baseline_record.search_query: type 2 diabetes AND pharmacotherapy AND randomized controlled trial
baseline_record.title: Efficacy of Gegen Qinlian decoction plus metformin for type 2 diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
baseline_record.abstract_summary: Gegen Qinlian Decoction (GQD) is frequently used as an adjunctive therapy to metformin for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), but the certainty and consistency of the supporting clinical evidence remain unclear. We searched CNKI, Wanfang Data, PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from database inception to January 31, 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing GQD plus metformin with metformin alone in adults with T2DM were included. The primary outcome was glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), and secondary outcomes were fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and 2-hour postprandial glucose (2hPG). Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed, with the primary analyses based on change-from-baseline values. Eight randomized controlled trials involving 725 participants were included. In the primary change-score analysis, GQD plus metformin did not show a statistically significant reduction in HbA1c compared with metformin alone (MD = -1.92, 95% CI: -4.43 to 0.59, P = 0.13). Statistically significant reductions were observed for FPG (MD = -1.08, 95% CI: -1.71 to -0.44, P = 0.0009) and 2hPG (MD = -1.73, 95% CI: -3.05 to -0.42, P = 0.010). However, substantial heterogeneity was present across analyses (I² = 85%–100%), and the certainty of evidence was rated as very low because of risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. Current evidence is insufficient to confirm a reliable clinical benefit of GQD as an adjunct to metformin for T2DM. Although reductions in FPG and 2hPG were observed, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory because of substantial heterogeneity, methodological limitations, and very low certainty of evidence. Larger, prospectively registered, well-designed, and adequately blinded randomized trials are needed.
baseline_record.notes: IMPORTANT: this is a systematic review/meta-analysis OF 8 RCTs, not a primary RCT itself. Good for testing retrieval on synthesis-heavy content (tables, GRADE ratings, forest plots) but the cluster needs at least one true primary-trial article for contrast in chunking behavior. Dense in numeric detail (MDs, CIs, I-squared values) -- good stress test for numeric fidelity in generation.

baseline_record.abstract_summary: The metabolic syndrome consists of central obesity, glucose intolerance, hyperinsulinemia, low high-density lipoproteins, high triglycerides and hypertension. Different studies have observed that metabolic syndrome causes microvascular complications in patients with type 2 diabetes. The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of metabolic syndrome in the Indian population with type 2 diabetes mellitus in relation to gender and duration of diabetes, and to evaluate the influence of metabolic syndrome and its individual components on microvascular complications such as diabetic retinopathy, diabetic nephropathy and diabetic neuropathy.
baseline_record.notes: Primary cross-sectional epidemiology study (1414 T2DM patients, South India), NOT a meta-analysis -- good contrast to diabetes-pharmacotherapy-rct.pdf for chunking variety. Heavy table density (7 tables of prevalence/OR data). Genuine overlap with the GQD article on terms like 'HbA1c' and 'type 2 diabetes complications', but different framing (risk-factor epidemiology vs. treatment efficacy) -- deliberately used as the cross-doc distractor pair, see golden_qa.json q008.

legacy_sources.title: Zinc, type 2 diabetes, diabetic kidney disease: focus on hypoxia

baseline_record.title: Zinc, type 2 diabetes, diabetic kidney disease: focus on hypoxia
baseline_record.abstract_summary: The incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus is approaching pandemic levels, posing a major global healthcare problem. Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the main cause of the chronic kidney disease. Hyperglycemia-dependent renal hypoxia drives the onset and progression of DKD. The adaptive cellular response to hypoxia depends on the zinc signalling, which promotes expression of the hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α). Zinc is further relevant for anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-fibrotic signalling pathways with nephroprotective effects in DKD. In this review, we focus on the role of zinc homeostasis in the development of diabetes and DKD, with particular emphasis on hypoxia as the central trigger of DKD. We also discuss the role of the zinc signaling in the cellular and systemic carbohydrate metabolism in the context of diabetes and DKD.
baseline_record.notes: Mechanistic/molecular review (zinc homeostasis, HIF-1a signalling, transporter biology), NOT a clinical trial or epidemiology study -- third distinct document type in the diabetes cluster, good for chunking variety. Dense with gene/protein names (ZnT1-8, ZIP1-14, HIF-1a/2a/3a, GPR39, NF-kB, etc.) and multiple detailed figures. Overlaps with diabetes-epidemiology-prevalence.pdf on 'diabetic nephropathy' and 'risk factors' but the framing differs sharply: statistical/epidemiological risk factors (Raman) vs. molecular pathogenic mechanism (this article) -- used as a second cross-doc distractor pair, see golden_qa.json q021. Explicitly states dosage/administration questions for zinc supplementation are out of scope -- good source for a scope-limited unanswerable query.

baseline_record.search_query: type 2 diabetes AND genetic risk AND GWAS
baseline_record.title: Disentangling Sex Differences in Sulfonylurea Drug Response With Genome-Wide Association Studies in Individuals With Type 2 Diabetes
baseline_record.abstract_summary: Sulfonylureas are a cornerstone of type 2 diabetes therapy despite interindividual variability in response. Despite well-documented sex-based differences, pharmacogenomic and genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have largely overlooked sex as a biological variable. We conducted the first sex-stratified GWAS of hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) response to sulfonylureas in Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes (ACCORD) clinical trial participants (N = 871). Variants meeting genome-wide (P < 5.0 × 10−8) and suggestive (P < 5.0 × 10−6) significance were assessed for replication in the Pharmacogenomics of Metformin (PMET1) cohort. Replicated variants were further analyzed in the Study to Understand the Genetics of the Acute Response to Metformin and Glipizide in Humans (SUGAR-MGH) cohort to assess acute insulin and glucose responses to a single glipizide dose. Genome-wide significant loci with sex-specific effects were identified: KAZN, KIF2B, SLC39A10, and SPINK5 (combined-sex); CRACR2A, KCNK2, and TENM2 (male-only); and NACPH2 (female-only). Two suggestive variants in the TMEM64/NECAB1 locus, associated with reduced HbA1c response to sulfonylureas in the male-only ACCORD analysis, were directly replicated in the PMET1 male-only cohort. In SUGAR-MGH, one replicated variant (rs6471250-C) was significantly associated with reduced peak insulin in males (P = 0.035) but not females (P = 0.40), demonstrating sex-specific functional effects. This study identified statistically supported and biologically plausible loci with prior evidence linking nearby genes to pathways relevant to sulfonylurea action, including insulin secretion, insulin regulation/sensitivity, calcium signaling, potassium-channel biology, and glucose transport. The findings highlight sex-specific differences in sulfonylurea response, providing mechanistic insights and underscoring the importance of sex-specific precision medicine. Identification of genetic variants influencing sex-specific response could inform dosing to optimize sulfonylureas.

legacy_sources.title: Sleep loss as a cardiometabolic risk factor: a narrative review of clinical and public health implications

baseline_record.title: Sleep loss as a cardiometabolic risk factor: a narrative review of clinical and public health implications
baseline_record.abstract_summary: Purpose: To synthesize current evidence on how sleep deprivation, impaired sleep architecture, and circadian misalignment affect cardiovascular and metabolic regulation across autonomic, hormonal, inflammatory, and behavioral pathways, and to highlight remaining research gaps in cardiometabolic sleep medicine. Methods: A structured literature search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar to identify peer-reviewed primary and review articles published within the past decade, using chronobiological and cardiometabolic search terms. Reference lists of retrieved articles were screened to identify additional relevant studies. Results: Experimental and epidemiologic data consistently link short or disturbed sleep with increased incidence of hypertension, coronary artery disease, stroke, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. Sleep loss activates the sympathetic nervous system and elevates cortisol, while suppressing growth hormone, thereby promoting vasoconstriction, endothelial dysfunction, and cardiac remodeling. Parallel disruption of leptin, ghrelin, and endocannabinoid signaling increases hunger, caloric intake, and preference for energy-dense foods, driving weight gain, visceral adiposity, and insulin resistance. Circadian misalignment from shift work and social jet lag further amplifies inflammatory signaling and metabolic risk across the lifespan. Limited interventional data suggest that sleep extension can improve appetite regulation, blood pressure, and some glycemic indices, but mechanistic and long-term outcomes remain underexplored. Conclusion: Sleep deprivation and circadian disruption mediate cardiometabolic disease through converging neuroendocrine, autonomic, inflammatory, and behavioral pathways. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and integrated multi-omics approaches combined with sleep phenotyping to clarify causal mechanisms and identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets in clinical sleep medicine.
baseline_record.notes: Narrative review (NOT systematic -- explicitly acknowledges no PRISMA protocol, no formal risk-of-bias assessment, 102 studies qualitatively synthesized). Primary lens is sleep/circadian biology, with T2DM and CVD outcomes as downstream topics rather than the central focus -- a looser fit for the 'cardiovascular outcomes' search slot than a dedicated CVD-in-diabetes study would be, but content coverage of HbA1c, metabolic syndrome, and CVD risk is substantial. Genuine overlap with diabetes-epidemiology-prevalence.pdf (Raman et al.) on metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular risk, but different framing: Raman = statistical prevalence/microvascular complications in existing diabetics; this review = sleep loss as a causal driver of MS and macrovascular (CAD/MI/stroke) risk. See golden_qa.json for the resulting distractor pair.

legacy_query.question: How does zinc modulate HIF-1a activity, and what downstream effect does this have on renal fibrosis in DKD?

expected_location.section: The role of zinc in the pathophysiology of DKD (and Figure 5)

legacy_query.reference_answer: Zinc induces HIF-1a proteasomal degradation and inhibits its translocation into the cell nucleus, preventing DNA binding and target gene transcription. This reduces activation of the HIF-1a/VEGF signalling pathway, decreasing angiogenesis, fibrosis, and inflammation. In animal DKD models, zinc administration reduced fibrotic markers and tubulointerstitial fibrosis via the PI3K/AKT/GSK-3b pathway, accompanied by decreased HIF-1a expression.

legacy_query.question: Compare the roles of ZnT7 and ZnT8 in protecting kidney tissue against diabetes-related fibrosis.

expected_location.section: The role of zinc in the pathophysiology of DKD

legacy_query.reference_answer: ZnT7 (localized in the perinuclear region/Golgi of rat kidney tubular cells) inhibits high-glucose-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) when overexpressed; its knockdown promotes EMT via activation of MAPK/ERK and TGF-b/Smad pathways. ZnT8 (predominantly in renal tubular epithelial cells) separately protects against EMT and tubulointerstitial fibrosis by restraining TGF-b1/Smads signalling, and additionally protects tubular cells from apoptosis via TNFAIP3-mediated suppression of NF-kB. Both transporters are renoprotective but act through distinct, non-identical signalling routes.

legacy_query.question: What is the molecular mechanism by which hyperglycemia leads to progression of diabetic kidney disease?

A retrieval system should favor the Lebedeva et al. mechanistic review here despite both documents using terms like 'diabetic nephropathy' and 'risk factors'.

legacy_query.question: What is the mechanistic link between ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels, calcium influx, and insulin secretion in pancreatic beta-cells?

expected_location.page: GWAS doc p.2 (Introduction, sulfonylurea mechanism); zinc/DKD review p.4-5 (SLC39A/ZIP transporters and ZnR/GPR39 sections)
expected_location.section: Complementary mechanistic descriptions in both documents

legacy_query.reference_answer: Both documents describe the same core mechanism from different angles. The GWAS paper explains that sulfonylureas bind the sulfonylurea receptor (SUR) on beta-cells, inhibit KATP channel potassium influx, depolarize the membrane, and trigger calcium influx that promotes insulin exocytosis; it also identifies genetic variants in calcium-signaling genes (CRACR2A, TMEM64/NECAB1) that modulate this pathway. The zinc/DKD review separately explains that zinc, acting as an intracellular signalling molecule, activates KATP channels at micromolar concentrations, suppressing calcium channel opening and providing a negative feedback loop on insulin release. A complete answer requires synthesizing both sources rather than treating either as sufficient alone.
legacy_query.notes: This is NOT a 'wrong-doc' distractor like q008/q021 -- it's a genuine cross-document synthesis case where the two sources are complementary rather than competing. Useful for testing whether the RAG system's agentic layer can retrieve and combine chunks from multiple documents for one answer, rather than only testing single-document precision.

cases.finding: Generic KATP/calcium question is answerable by the zinc review alone; current question does not demand attributed complementary facts from both papers. Gold copies GWAS potassium influx wording; do not endorse as established physiology. New synthesis must explicitly require distinct article-specific facts.

legacy_query.question: Which racial/ethnic group showed significantly better HbA1c response to sulfonylureas compared to non-Hispanic Black individuals?

expected_location.section: Results (opening paragraph) and Figure 1

legacy_query.reference_answer: Non-Hispanic White (NHW) individuals showed significantly better response than non-Hispanic Black (NHB) individuals (P=0.0013). No significant difference was found between NHW and Hispanic individuals (P=0.14).

cases.finding: NHW/NHB P=.0013 and NHW/Hispanic P=.14 supported but ancestry/race covariate association is not genetic causality. Restricted source excluded; preserve population differentiation in another case.

legacy_query.question: How many studies were included in the final qualitative synthesis of this narrative review, and what search methodology was used?

expected_location.section: Methods

legacy_query.reference_answer: 102 studies were included. The authors searched PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar using chronobiology- and cardiometabolic-related keywords/MeSH terms, prioritizing the past 10 years. This was a narrative review, not a systematic review -- no PRISMA protocol was used, and intermediate screening counts were not prospectively recorded.

cases.finding: 102 studies and narrative/non-PRISMA method supported; no prospective intermediate screening counts. Explicit review identity and no systematic-review claim.

legacy_query.question: What increase in myocardial infarction and stroke risk was found by Cappuccio et al. (2011) for habitual short sleep (<6 hours) in a large longitudinal study?

expected_location.section: Results > Sleep deprivation and cardiovascular disease

legacy_query.reference_answer: Habitual sleep duration under 6 hours per night was associated with a 48% higher risk of developing and/or dying from heart disease and a 15% increased chance of developing and/or dying from stroke, based on data from over 474,000 participants across 8 countries.

cases.finding: Review attributes 48% heart-disease and 15% stroke increased developing/dying risk to pooled longitudinal evidence. Question incorrectly singles out MI and a single large study; revise to review-attributed heart-disease endpoints, not new primary-trial evidence.

legacy_query.question: How did fasting glucose, insulin, and insulin sensitivity change with sleep extension in the Leproult et al. study?

expected_location.section: Results > Sleep loss and cardiometabolic disease

legacy_query.reference_answer: There was no significant change in overall insulin and glucose levels before versus after sleep extension. However, percent changes were more pronounced with sleep extension: a positive correlation for glucose (r=+0.53, P=0.041) and a negative correlation for insulin (r=-0.60, P=0.025). Insulin sensitivity improved significantly with sleep extension (r=+0.76, P=0.002).

cases.finding: Leproult 16 healthy non-obese adults: no overall glucose/insulin change, correlations with sleep extension reported. Avoid equating positive glucose correlation with desirable glucose reduction or calling a correlation an intervention effect size.

legacy_query.question: What hormonal mechanisms link sleep deprivation to both increased appetite/obesity risk and impaired glucose metabolism?

expected_location.section: Sleep loss and metabolic syndrome; Sleep problems and the development of obesity

legacy_query.reference_answer: Sleep loss increases ghrelin and reduces leptin (raising the ghrelin/leptin ratio), which drives hunger and caloric intake. It also upregulates the endocannabinoid system, further increasing appetite and craving for energy-dense foods. Separately, sleep restriction disrupts cortisol secretion (evening rise, slower decline, higher nadir), which affects glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity. Experimentally, one week of sleep restriction produced a 40% drop in glucose clearance rate and a 30% lower insulin response on an intravenous glucose tolerance test, comparable to a prediabetic state -- linking the same hormonal disruption to both appetite dysregulation and impaired glucose handling.

cases.finding: Appetite/endocannabinoid and cortisol/glucose mechanisms require separate review locations. Frame as reviewed mechanisms from different cited experiments, not proof that one hormonal change caused every reported endpoint.

legacy_query.question: According to the evidence reviewed, what relative risks of coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, and stroke are associated with metabolic syndrome?

expected_location.section: Results > Sleep loss and cardiometabolic disease (citing Isomaa et al. 2001)

legacy_query.reference_answer: Citing Isomaa et al. (2001), metabolic syndrome significantly increased the risk of coronary artery disease, MI, and stroke, with relative risks of 2.96, 2.63, and 2.27 respectively (P<0.001). This is distinct from the Raman et al. epidemiology study, which examines metabolic syndrome's association with MICROvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) in an existing diabetic population, not these macrovascular relative risks. A retrieval system should favor this sleep/cardiometabolic review for a question specifically about CAD/MI/stroke risk ratios, despite both documents discussing metabolic syndrome extensively.
legacy_query.notes: Third cross-doc distractor pair in the diabetes cluster. Same underlying confusability pattern as q008/q021: shared vocabulary ('metabolic syndrome', 'cardiovascular risk') but different outcome focus (macrovascular RRs here vs. microvascular complication prevalence in Raman et al.).

cases.finding: 2.96/2.63/2.27 review-attributed macrovascular risks supported; current generic evidence-reviewed question can accept alternatives. Explicitly identify review/cited cohort; use eligible prevalence paper as competing population/outcome evidence.

legacy_query.question: What effect did daylight saving time transitions have on myocardial infarction rates, according to the Sadhu et al. analysis discussed in this review?

expected_location.section: Results > Sleep deprivation and cardiovascular disease

legacy_query.reference_answer: The spring transition (losing ~1 hour of sleep) was associated with a 24% increase in MIs the following day (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.05-1.46, P=0.011). The fall transition (gaining ~1 hour of sleep) was associated with a 21% decrease in MIs the following day (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.62-0.99, P=0.044). The review notes these findings should be interpreted cautiously given modest, transient effect sizes and some conflicting more recent large-scale studies.

cases.finding: Review reports day-specific spring/fall MI changes and no weekly PCI-for-MI change; original wording omits weekly null result and location is stale. Preserve reviewed observational/natural-experiment scope and conflicting literature caveat.

legacy_query.question: What retrieval architecture (vector index, chunking strategy, embedding model) did the conversational agent system in this study use?

expected_location.section: Methods > CA Design

legacy_query.reference_answer: Documents were split into approximately 500-character segments with 100-character overlap using a recursive character-based splitter, embedded using OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small model, and stored in a FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) vector index. At inference time, the top 2 nearest segments (top_k=2) were retrieved by L2 (Euclidean) distance using the current question as the query.
legacy_query.notes: SANITY-CHECK CASE: this is the only document in the corpus discussing RAG/vector-retrieval architecture at all. No other document should plausibly compete for this query -- if retrieval pulls from any other document for this question, that's a clear signal of a retrieval pipeline problem, not genuine ambiguity.

cases.finding: FAISS, 500/100 characters, text-embedding-3-small, top_k=2 and L2 supported. Name Guo CGM counseling study; its RAG architecture does not establish patient outcomes. Original note that any unrelated returned chunk proves a pipeline problem is too absolute.

legacy_query.question: How accurately could clinicians identify whether a given response was written by the CA or a human clinician, and what does this imply about the source-masking design?

expected_location.section: Results > Safety and Source Identification; Discussion > Limitations

legacy_query.reference_answer: Among definitive judgments, overall identification accuracy was 87.5%, significantly above the 50% chance level (P<.001). Five of six clinicians showed high discrimination accuracy (82.3%-100%), while one performed at chance. This means that although the rating task was source-masked by design, responses were often practically distinguishable in practice -- likely due to consistent CA response style, structure, and length -- which the authors explicitly flag as a limitation affecting how the quality comparison should be interpreted.

cases.finding: 797 definitive judgments versus all 864 ratings is essential: 87.5% versus 80.7% correct overall, 67 unsure. Results/Limitations support imperfect practical masking and familiarity bias, not a causal source-bias estimate. Require separate result and limitation anchors.
